//: A counter is where you would get this if you were not making it at home — the kind of place a person recognises from their own street. A recipe can sit at several, because noodles are not only sold by the sushi-and-ramen place, so `counters` on a recipe is a list. `categories` here is a fallback only: a recipe that names no counter lands at whichever counters claim its category, so nothing is ever orphaned. The fallbacks are deliberately coarse — they exist so the build never drops a recipe, not because every brownie belongs at the same shelf — and they are meant to be replaced recipe by recipe with a `>> counters:` line. Counters with no fallback are filled in by hand; a counter with nothing on it simply does not render. The archetypes and the menu vocabulary behind them are recorded in docs/knowledge/counters.md. A section may also carry `notes`, which is shelf talk: a sentence comparing the things on this shelf, which is the one comparison a recipe page cannot make because it can only show you one of them. An entry with `of` is about that dish and prints beside it; one without is about the section and prints under its heading. Both are optional, both are one sentence, and scripts/parse-recipes.mjs will not let a note point at a slug this section does not shelve. They are the only thing in this file written by hand rather than derived, so scripts/menu-sections.mjs --write — which rebuilds `sections` from docs/gaps/*.md — will drop every one of them.

notes.note: These arrive before you have ordered: the tray is mango chutney, lime pickle, mint sauce and raw onion.
The plate of raw onion that comes with the papadoms: cold sharp and crunchy against ten sauces that are none of those.
The sweet corner of the tray and the one that goes on the papadom first. Better after a fortnight.
What you reach for when a vindaloo has gone wrong, and half the meal beside a biryani.
What the tandoori marinade was written for. The same skewers dropped into a makhani gravy are butter chicken.
The only line here finished with fresh mint, and the only one cooked fast in a thin steel bowl.
The driest line here and the one to order if you are eating with bread rather than rice.
The only line here that is a stir-fry and not a simmer, and the vinegar at the end is why it tastes sharper.
The mildest line here and the one to order when you cannot judge a kitchen yet.
The second-hottest line here: hotter than a bhuna and below a vindaloo, and sour with tamarind as well as hot.
The other mild line beside korma, told apart by almonds ground and stirred in rather than blended to a cream.
Not a stirred rice — rice mixed into curry is a pulao, and the difference is exactly this lid.
The rice that comes with everything, and not the tiffin counter's lemon rice up the page.
The same tomato and cashews as the tikka masala gravy; the difference is the butter in cold at the end.
Nine lines on the sauce list start here: bhuna dopiaza jalfrezi madras vindaloo karahi balti dansak patia.

notes.note: Every one is written for low and six to eight hours. Nothing browns in a sealed crock, so colour comes before or after.
The only one here that browns before the pot: a wing is an awkward shape to turn in a pan, and a sheet tray does four.
The one here that is not leave-it-and-go — you are home for the last two hours, adding the vegetables in order.
The one here with the most room in it: a pot that tops out at a simmer cannot overcook a cheek.
All day with a hock is how greens are actually cooked, so the machine matches the method rather than shortening it.
The pot cannot exceed a bare shiver, which is what this cut wants — pressure shreds a brisket before the cabbage.
The easiest one here: nothing is browned, nothing goes in late, and there is no pan to wash.
The shortest braise here at six hours, and the one where longer is actively worse.
The one bean dish here where slow beats pressure outright — a crock is the closest vessel to a bean pot there is.
The shortest cook here, four hours, and the only one where longer is actively worse.
